questions.q: If Opportunity has two separate before-insert triggers, what does Salesforce guarantee about the order they run in?
options: Nothing — the relative execution order between separate triggers on the same object/event is not guaranteed
They always run in alphabetical order by trigger name
They always run in the order they were created
The shorter trigger always runs first
questions.explain: Salesforce allows multiple triggers per object and event, but does not guarantee the order they execute in relative to each other.

questions.q: What is the main risk of unguaranteed execution order between two triggers on the same object?
options: The org will fail to deploy
Logic that depends on running before or after other logic can produce different, hard-to-reproduce results depending on order
Only one of the two triggers will ever actually fire
SOQL queries inside the triggers will return stale data
questions.explain: When one trigger's result depends on another's having (or not having) already run, an unguaranteed order means the outcome can vary and the bug can be nearly impossible to reproduce consistently.

questions.q: What is Salesforce's recommended practice for handling multiple pieces of logic on the same object?
options: Write a new trigger for every new requirement
Avoid triggers entirely and use only Flow
One trigger per object, covering all its events, delegating to a handler where execution order is explicit in code
Always name triggers alphabetically so order is predictable
questions.explain: Consolidating to one trigger per object, with a handler controlling call order explicitly, removes the platform's unguaranteed ordering from the equation.

questions.q: When consolidating several existing triggers on one object into a single trigger, what's a safe approach?
options: Delete all the old triggers first, then write the new one from memory
Move each old trigger's logic into its own handler method, call them in a deliberate order, then deactivate the old triggers one at a time while testing
Leave the old triggers active alongside the new consolidated one
Rename the old triggers but keep their bodies unchanged
questions.explain: A mechanical, incremental migration — moving logic into handler methods and deactivating old triggers one at a time with testing in between — avoids losing logic or breaking behavior mid-migration.

questions.q: In the handler-based consolidated trigger, how is call order between two pieces of logic (like applying a discount and then calculating commission) controlled?
options: It can't be controlled; Salesforce still decides it internally
By which method name comes first alphabetically
By which trigger event is listed first in the trigger definition
By an explicit sequence of method calls written in the handler's code
questions.explain: Once both pieces of logic are methods called from a single handler, the order is simply the order those calls are written in code — fully explicit and under the developer's control.
